Jiri Strejc
yee'ree straytz
n. (Jiri Strejc, 1536–1599, Brethren minister, Czech psalmist and translator of the Kralice Bible)
Czech Jiri from Greek Georgios, a husbandman; Strejc, an uncle, a kinsman, a Czech surname.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Jiri Strejc, known in Latin as Georgius Vetter, was a minister of the Unity of the Brethren in Moravia who did two things that outlived him. He was one of the translators of the Kralice Bible, the Brethren's six-volume Czech Scriptures made from Hebrew and Greek with commentary and published between 1579 and 1593 — the Czech Bible, as the Authorized Version is the English one, and for three hundred years the standard of the written language. And in 1587 he put the Genevan Psalter into Czech verse, keeping the French tunes, so that Czech-speaking Protestants sang what Geneva, Hungary and the Netherlands sang. The dictionary pairs him deliberately with Albert Szenci Molnar in Hungary and with the Dutch and French psalters: the same melodies, the same hundred and fifty psalms, carried into four or five languages within a generation by men who never met. That is what a confessional communion actually looks like, and it was built out of a text and a tune rather than out of a council.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines psalmody as the practice of singing psalms, and tune as a series of musical notes in a particular measure.

expand to see more

PSAL'MODY, n. The act, practice or art of singing sacred songs.

TUNE, n. A series of musical notes in some particular measure, and consisting of a single series.

VER'SION, n. A translation; that which is rendered from another language.

COM'MENTARY, n. A series of comments or annotations; an exposition of a book.

Modern Corruption

He translated for the Kralice Bible and set the Genevan Psalter to Czech verse in 1587.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that Christian unity has to be organised from a centre. Nobody organised the spread of the Genevan Psalter. Czech, Hungarian, Dutch, German and English congregations ended up singing the same tunes to the same hundred and fifty psalms because each independently judged that the Psalter is the church's songbook and the tunes were serviceable.

The principle to recover is that the Psalms are given for all nations to sing and that singing them is itself a confession of one faith. “O sing unto the LORD a new song: sing unto the LORD, all the earth” (Psa 96:1). The shortest psalm commands it of the heathen: “O praise the LORD, all ye nations: praise him, all ye people” (Psa 117:1). And the end of it is seen in John's vision of “a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues” (Rev 7:9).

Usage

"“sing unto the LORD, all the earth” (Psa 96:1) — the Genevan tunes set to Czech verse in 1587."

"“O praise the LORD, all ye nations” (Psa 117:1) — the same psalter in Czech, Hungarian, Dutch and French."

"“of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues” (Rev 7:9) — six volumes of the Kralice Bible."
